title: 2026 Global AI Jobs Barometer (press release)
key_claim: Analysing more than one billion job ads in 27 countries, PwC finds AI is creating a two-track labour market: the average wage premium for AI skills rose to 62% (up from 57%), professionalised roles see twice the job growth and 42% faster salary growth than democratised roles, the top 20% most AI-exposed firms posted 163% labour-productivity growth, and AI-exposed entry-level roles grew 35% since 2019 while other entry-level roles shrank 10% as routine apprenticeship tasks are automated.
frame_summary: Argues that AI is splitting the labour market into two tracks and rewarding human judgement, with AI skills commanding a rising wage premium while routine entry tasks that once built expertise are automated away.
verbatim_quote: the average wage premium for workers with AI skills continued to surge higher - hitting 62%, up from 57% last year. 'Professionalised' roles ... are seeing twice the growth in available jobs and 42% faster salary growth than those categorised as 'democratised'. The top 20% of the most AI-exposed companies achieved average labour productivity growth of 163% relative to 2018. Job openings for these 'seniorised' entry-level roles have grown 35% since 2019, while other entry-level roles shrank 10%.
notes: Primary anchor: skill churn, AI wage premium and the automation of apprenticeship tasks.

title: Annual Skills Report 2026 (Landmark report sets out action to address key skills gaps)
key_claim: The UK government skills body warns the skills system is falling behind the pace of economic and technological change: demand in priority sectors will grow about 24% over the next decade (up to 1.8 million additional workers), reskilling and upskilling are essential, AI will affect almost every job but future skill needs are uncertain, and the long-term decline in employer investment in training continues while SMEs struggle to engage.
frame_summary: Argues that England's skills system is failing to keep pace with a fast-changing, AI-affected economy, and that the long-run decline in employer training investment is a central obstacle.
verbatim_quote: demand in priority sectors will grow by 24% over the next decade ... up to 1.8 million additional workers will be needed to meet this demand ... The long-term decline in employer investment continues and SMEs struggle to engage in the skills system ... AI will affect almost every job and sector, but the pace of this change and the future skills requirements are uncertain.
notes: Tier 1 government anchor for the employer-training-decline and pace-of-change claims.

title: Making AI Work: Why Investing in Skills Matters
date_evidence: OECD blog; canonical URL .../blogs/2026/01/making-ai-work-why-investing-in-skills-matters.html; published January 2026
key_claim: OECD argues that skills are the binding constraint on AI's productivity payoff: skills gaps are slowing AI adoption, AI is reshaping employer skill demand, and training is key to good outcomes, yet training supply may be insufficient for general AI-literacy needs and the workers most exposed to automation are least likely to access training, requiring shared responsibility among employers, workers and governments.
frame_summary: Argues that investing in skills and training is the decisive lever for AI to deliver productivity and inclusive outcomes, and that current training supply and access are falling short.
notes: Structural anchor (3-6m): canonical OECD framing that training is the key and is not keeping up.

title: The 2026 AI Index Report, Economy chapter
date_evidence: Multiple sources confirm the 2026 AI Index Report was published on April 13, 2026; report page header '04 Economy | The 2026 AI Index Report'.
key_claim: Stanford's 2026 AI Index finds AI's labour-market effects concentrated in hiring pipelines and the youngest workers: employment for software developers aged 22 to 25 has fallen nearly 20% from 2024, one-third of surveyed organisations expect AI to reduce their workforce in the coming year, and measured productivity gains are largest in structured, monitorable work.
frame_summary: Argues that AI's measured labour-market impact is so far uneven and concentrated on early-career workers in exposed occupations, with broad productivity gains still limited to structured tasks.
verbatim_quote: Employment for software developers ages 22 to 25 has fallen nearly 20% from 2024. ... One-third of organizations expect AI to reduce their workforce in the coming year.
notes: Corroborates the erosion of early-career rungs in exposed occupations.

title: Reskilling Revolution on Track to Reach over 850 Million People (press release)
key_claim: At Davos the WEF reported its Reskilling Revolution initiative has mobilised commitments to reach 856 million people by 2030 (toward a one-billion goal), with more than 25 technology companies pledging to support 120 million workers, while new WEF-PwC research surveying 9,000 entry-level workers across 48 countries reveals widespread uncertainty about skills relevance and job security.
frame_summary: Argues that a large, coordinated global reskilling effort is mobilising at scale to prepare workers for the AI economy.
verbatim_quote: World Economic Forum Reskilling Revolution on track to reach over 850 million people. The Reskilling Revolution initiative has mobilized commitments to reach 856 million people globally by 2030 ... more than 25 technology companies have pledged to support 120 million workers with AI access, skills training and job pathways.
notes: Counter-argument anchor: the reskilling push is real and large-scale.

title: How AI is Changing Early Careers: A View from Entry-Level Workers (Executive Briefing)
date_evidence: PDF title page: 'How AI is Changing Early Careers: A View from Entry-Level Workers EXECUTIVE BRIEFING JANUARY 2026'
key_claim: Drawing on PwC's Global Workforce Hopes and Fears survey of 9,394 entry-level employees across 48 countries, the WEF-PwC briefing finds AI is automating the routine tasks that traditionally helped newcomers build confidence and expertise, that entry-level workers are the cohort least likely to feel last year's learning helped their career (57%) and only 53% feel their manager supports capability-building, even as roles increasingly demand judgement and adaptability from the start.
frame_summary: Argues that AI is redefining entry-level work by removing the routine tasks that once formed on-the-job apprenticeship, leaving early-career workers uncertain about the durability of their skills.
verbatim_quote: it removes the structured, repetitive tasks that traditionally helped them build confidence and understand workplace culture ... only 53% of entry-level workers strongly agree that their manager supports them in building new capabilities.
notes: Mechanism source: the automation of apprenticeship tasks and doubts over skill shelf-life.

title: Human skills increasingly in demand as AI reshapes labour market, PwC finds
key_claim: Reporting on PwC's Barometer, Euronews notes jobs requiring specific AI expertise have grown 69% since 2019 (almost eight times the 9% growth of the wider jobs market) and the AI-skills wage premium has reached 62%, ranging from as high as 118% in consumer markets to 16% in government and public sector roles.
frame_summary: Reports that demand and pay for AI and human skills are rising sharply and unevenly as AI reshapes the labour market, widening gaps between AI-fluent and other workers.
verbatim_quote: The average wage premium attached to AI skills has also increased to 62%, the report found. The wage premium varies significantly by industry, reaching as high as 118% in consumer markets and falling to 16% in government and public sector roles.
notes: Independent journalism corroboration of the AI-fluency pay divide.
